newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T holds ground on U.S. tobacco deal.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T holds ground on U.S. tobacco deal.

text.p: Martin Broughton, chief executive of British-based B.A.T Industries Plc, said on Wednesday he would accept no fundamental changes to a proposed settlement between the U.S. tobacco industry and state attorneys.
"It's a package. In essence, take it or leave it. If you are looking for fundamental change, then no," he told Reuters in an interview.

He also said that there was little advantage in a "straight demerger" of the group's financial services business because of "financial inefficiencies" and the company "would need to await more clarity on FIDS."

American tobacco companies agreed with state attorneys in June to settle most legal claims against them over smoking in return for payments totalling 230 billion stg over 25 years, along with tougher regulation of products and advertising.
The landmark settlement, which would also give companies immunity from most future claims, still awaits approval from Congress.
"We signed up to things we don't like -- it's a package," said Broughton.

When asked if B.A.T would accept restrictions on the sale of cigarettes oustide the U.S. under these proposals, he replied: "There is a tendency in the U.S. to seek to take extra-territorial jursidiction. America should look after America and keep its nose out of anywhere else."
The UK government plans to abolish FIDS -- Foreign Income Dividends -- from 1999, but has said there could be concessions after protests from British-based international companies.
FIDS allow companies to avoid paying tax in Britain on earnings already taxed abroad that are distributed as dividends.

Companies say the abolition of FIDS would mean that they are effectively taxed twice on profits earned abroad -- once by the foreign country involved and then with Advance Corporation Tax (ACT) in Britain.

There has been continuing speculation in the investment community that B.A.T will demerge its financial services business, which has gained further strength now its U.S. tobacco subsidiary, Brown & Williamson, has apparently removed some legal uncertainties with the landmark industry deal.
